# Forensic Dossier — Amadeus IT Group, S.A. (AMS.MC)

*Interrogator: Claude Opus 4.8 · Investment Committee · Transcripts FY2024 results (2025-02-28) through Q3-2025 (2025-11-07), cross-referenced against the screener financial trajectory and live 2026 facts.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across four consecutive calls the core story is strikingly **stable in substance and steadily shifting in register**. The spine never changes: Amadeus is the B2B technology rail of global travel — Air Distribution (the GDS/Travel Platform), Airline IT (Altéa/Navitaire passenger systems, now Nevio retailing), and Hospitality & Other Solutions (ACRS central-reservation, payments, media). What evolves is *which leg carries the narrative weight* and *how defensively management frames the macro*.

- **FY2024 call (2025-02-28) — peak offense.** Maroto opens on "double digit growth and expanding profitability," 13% revenue, 13% EBITDA, FCF €1.3B (+16%), leverage 0.9x. The two load-bearing growth stories are (a) **NDC aggregation** ("we aim to become the undisputed aggregator of NDC content," 70+ agreements) and (b) **Nevio**, the next-gen airline retailing platform, with Air France-KLM joining British Airways, Saudia and Finnair as a fourth signed customer. Hospitality is framed as a land-grab (Marriott, Accor, MGM implementations). Capital allocation headline: a fresh **€1.3B buyback** to mop up the 2020 convertible/equity-raise dilution.
- **Q1-2025 (2025-05-08) — first defensive notes.** New CFO Carol Borg debuts. Group revenue +9%, but the tone introduces hedging: "Despite the broad uncertainty in the environment," bookings growth decelerating (Travel Platform bookings +3% vs +9% in Q4-24), management pivots to reporting **ex-ForEx** because "high USD-euro exchange rate volatility beyond what we could foresee." FCF down 22% YoY on CapEx/working-capital/tax timing — the first time the cash-flow narrative needs *defending* rather than *celebrating*.
- **H1-2025 (2025-08-01) — narrative simplification + macro management.** Management explicitly "made some changes to our quarterly presentation… to simplify how we communicate." Revenue +8% cc. The story leans harder on **cloud transformation** (90% of apps in public cloud) and **AI/Agentic AI** as the forward narrative, and on Google/Microsoft partnerships. A telling admission: traffic "progressive deterioration" through the half (April > May > June), with the bull pivot being "hopefully, we have seen the bottom."
- **Q3-2025 (2025-11-07) — re-acceleration claim + AI offense.** "Strong third quarter full of momentum, which drove revenue growth acceleration and margin expansion." New customer wins (Ascott in hospitality; Qatar, Vietnam, Jazeera, Singapore Airlines in revenue management). The forward narrative is now overwhelmingly **AI/Agentic AI** ("over 500 potential use cases," "first data mesh in travel"), a deliberate re-framing of the company as an AI-leverage story rather than a cyclical-bookings story.

**Quietly dropped / softened:** the *bookings-volume* growth story faded from hero to footnote as 2025 air-traffic normalized; by Q3 the emphasis migrated to revenue-per-unit (price/booking +5%, rev-per-PB +5%) and IT/hospitality structural growth. **Newly introduced:** AI/Agentic AI as the central forward thesis, and Navitaire Stratos (the low-cost-carrier sibling to Nevio).

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | Financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Double digit growth… FCF €1.3B (+16%)" | FY24 | Rev 6.14B(2024)→6.52B(2025); NI 1.25B→1.34B; 3yr rev CAGR +13.3%; FCF 3yr CAGR +33.8% | **Corroborated.** The growth was real and cash-backed. |
| "Profit grew faster than revenues" | H1-25 | Net margin 20.5%, FCF margin 32.1%; EPS +7.9% YoY on rev +6.1% | **Corroborated** — operating leverage is real, EPS outgrew revenue. |
| "Expanding profitability / margin expansion" | Q3-25 | But scan flags **Gross margin 27.8% (contracting)**; margin 0.57σ *below* historical peak | **Partial divergence.** Reported EBIT margin expands, yet gross margin is contracting and the company sits below its own peak-margin — investment (R&D ~20% of revenue, cloud migration) is compressing the gross line even as operating leverage flatters EBIT. |
| "Strong commercial momentum… acceleration" | Q3-25 | Rev growth slowed to +6.1% YoY (2025) from +13% (2024); fwd EPS growth +11.4% | **Story richer than the print.** "Acceleration" is constant-currency and segment-cherry-picked; the reported top line *decelerated* hard from 2024's pace. |
| Buyback to "repurchase and redeem all… shares" from 2020 raise | FY24/Q1-25 | Net debt 2.68B (live, 2026-03-31), leverage ~1.0x; €500M new program Mar–Jun 2026 | **Corroborated but modest.** Real, disciplined, dilution-offsetting — *not* a balance-sheet-transforming return. |
| "Beat 6/7 quarters (86%)" | — | Screener earnings-beat rate 86%; EPS 3yr CAGR +27.6% | **Corroborated.** Genuine guidance-delivery track record. |

**Net read:** the financials *support* the durability claim (recurring, high-FCF, 86% beat rate, EPS CAGR +27.6%) but *do not* support the "acceleration" framing — 2025 was a **deceleration year** (rev +6.1% vs +13.3% 3yr CAGR) dressed in constant-currency language. The story is modestly *richer* than the reported trajectory, mostly via the cc/ex-ForEx lens and segment selection.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-mildly-Declining offense, with a deliberate Q3 re-offensive pivot to AI.**

- FY24 (Rising/peak): "highly productive year… delivered on our outlook and commitments." Unhedged.
- Q1-25 (First hedge): "Despite the broad uncertainty… we are focusing our '25 outlook excluding ForEx effects." Volumes "a bit below… but nevertheless quite good."
- H1-25 (Most defensive): "challenging macro and geopolitical environment"; repeated "hopefully we have seen the bottom"; FCF deterioration "expected" in H1, recovery promised in H2. This is the low point of confidence — management is managing *down* expectations on volumes and *up* on H2 hope.
- Q3-25 (Re-offensive): "strong… full of momentum… revenue growth acceleration." The defensiveness recedes; the company re-frames around AI leadership ("almost 20 years," "500 use cases," "uniquely placed to infuse Agentic AI").

The shift from **offensive (NDC/Nevio land-grab)** to **defensive (ForEx/macro/cloud-cost)** language in mid-2025, then a **re-offensive AI re-frame** in Q3, is the key tonal signature. Guidance specificity *decreased* (moved to cc/ex-ForEx framing, simplified presentation) — a mild credibility cost.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** The screener corroborates an **86% earnings-beat rate (6/7)** and an EPS 3-yr CAGR of +27.6% against a guided trajectory management consistently described as "delivered on our outlook." When H1-2025 disappointed on volumes/FCF, management did *not* cut full-year guidance — they reaffirmed the **ex-ForEx outlook** and pointed to an H2 recovery, and the Q3 print ("revenue growth acceleration") and the **maintained FY2026 guidance** (live: Q1-2026 +7.9% cc, within ranges) suggest the H2 promise broadly held. The one credibility wrinkle is the *re-basing to constant-currency* mid-year, which makes the "delivered" claim less falsifiable. No evidence of systematic sandbagging — beats are modest (latest-Q EPS +5% YoY), consistent with honest, slightly-conservative guidance rather than lowballing.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Nevio/Stratos conversion pace (recurring, escalating).** Sven Merkt (H1-25): "what the main obstacles are to converting these deals." James Goodall (Q3-25, sharper): "we haven't seen a new customer for a while and Nevio still waiting for one on Stratos. Are you comfortable with the current pace?" Management's answer — "engagement is high… nothing is done until it's really done" — is a **classic non-answer deflection**. This was the single most-pressed worry and it later resolved *positively* (live 2026: TUI signed as Navitaire Stratos launch customer; Lufthansa Group adopted Nevio).
- **Free-cash-flow deterioration (Q1/H1-25).** Toby Ogg pushed twice on FCF down 22% and the H2 reacceleration "building blocks." Maroto's answer leaned on "seasonality… working capital… taxes" — vague, but the H2 recovery did materialize.
- **Booking-fee pricing durability.** Laurent Daure repeatedly probed whether the +5% rev/booking is structural or a one-off from full-content→free-negotiation contract resets. Management conceded the contract-reset tailwind "probably will not be there" — an honest admission that a pricing lever is maturing.
- **Hospitality guidance (payments/Marriott ramp).** Analysts repeatedly questioned the H2 acceleration needed to hit the low end; management blamed media/US sentiment and a payments-implementation delay — a recurring soft spot.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Gross margin contracting** (27.8%, below historical peak) while R&D runs ~20% of revenue and cloud migration costs persist — heavy reinvestment is masking gross-line pressure.
🔴 **Constant-currency re-framing** mid-2025 reduced guidance falsifiability; "acceleration" claims rest on cc + segment selection while reported growth decelerated.
🔴 **Pricing-lever maturation** — management openly conceded the contract-reset booking-fee tailwind fades.
🔴 **AI/agentic look-to-book risk** — GDS CEOs (incl. Amadeus) have publicly said AI is worsening look-to-book ratios; the AI-as-disintermediation tail is now an *acknowledged* industry debate, not a fringe fear.
🟢 **86% beat rate, EPS CAGR +27.6%, FCF CAGR +33.8%** — genuine, cash-backed delivery.
🟢 **Switching-cost moat intact** — airline IT (Altéa/Nevio) and hospitality CRS are multi-year, mission-critical, sticky migrations (Marriott, Accor, MGM, Ascott live/ramping).
🟢 **Nevio/Stratos worry resolved** — the most-pressed analyst concern (conversion pace) reversed positively in 2026 (TUI Stratos, Lufthansa Nevio).
🟢 **Deleveraged** — net debt/EBITDA ~1.0x, FCF margin 32%, Piotroski 7/9, Altman-Z 3.0 (solvent).

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Terminology migration from "bookings" to "AI/data mesh."** Across the four calls the unit of pride shifts from *volume* (bookings, PBs) to *technology leverage* (cloud %, AI use-cases, data mesh). This is partly genuine strategy and partly a **defensive re-narration** away from a maturing/cyclical volume story toward an open-ended AI TAM ("we have not revisited the €41B TAM… in theory it should extend").
- **Capital-allocation language hardening.** Borg (Q3-25) gives the disciplined-capital-allocation catechism — organic investment first, dividend, *then* "M&A still remains… a key relevant part of our growth strategy" and "we'll come back in February" with any change. This telegraphs that the buyback is a *bridge* (dilution mop-up), not a new permanent return policy, and that **bolt-on M&A** remains the preferred use of cash — a mild negative for those hoping for accelerating shareholder returns.
- **New CFO voice.** Borg is more precise on cost/cloud-lapping mechanics ("lapping of Vision-Box consolidation," "slowdown in underlying cost growth in FY26") — a more controlled, finance-led narration than Maroto's commercial-optimism register. The CFO change reads as a professionalization, not a red flag.
- **Disintermediation candor.** In Q3, management volunteered that historical direct-sell disintermediation "is clearly a reality" but "we are seeing less in '25" — an honest framing that the structural headwind exists but is being offset by share gains and content-onboarding.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE** (a high-quality, cash-compounding infrastructure franchise in a deceleration-then-stabilization phase, re-narrating around AI). Not strengthening (growth decelerated from 2024's pace; gross margin contracting; pricing lever maturing), not deteriorating (delivery track record intact, moat sticky, deleveraged, the key analyst worry resolved positively in 2026).

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is a **quality-compounder-at-a-discount, not a special-situation.** The "catalyst" (the €500M buyback running Mar–Jun 2026) is small (~1.6% of market cap, ~3.5% of shares), serial, and dilution-offsetting — already substantially executed and re-rate-spent. The real question is whether the **AI/agentic-distribution debate** (look-to-book degradation; direct-retailing/tech-native disintermediation) is a *fear-print mispricing* on an entrenched switching-cost rail, or the early innings of a *terminal* erosion of the GDS toll-booth. The financials say the moat is **paying** (32% FCF margin, ROIC ~9.9%, sticky multi-year IT/CRS contracts), but the gross-margin contraction and the look-to-book candor say the franchise is **investing hard to stay ahead** of that threat — so the value case rests on the threat being *manageable* (re-platforming captures the shift) rather than *terminal* (rails get disintermediated).

**MOAT:** Type = **switching-costs + network/scale** (airline-IT migrations are multi-year and mission-critical; the Travel Platform is a two-sided air-content/travel-seller network; GDS scale economics). Width: **WIDE but with a contracting gross margin** — ROIC ~9.9% is solid-not-spectacular and roughly stable, FCF conversion is elite, but the gross line is eroding under reinvestment. I read the durable earnings base as wide; the *trend* is the watch-item.
**MOAT_TREND:** **STABLE** — returns and FCF conversion are holding; gross margin is contracting on reinvestment (cloud + R&D 20% of sales), but that reinvestment is defending and extending the moat (Nevio/Stratos/AI), not a sign of collapse. Not yet eroding at the franchise level.
**SECULAR_THREAT:** **manageable** — AI/agentic distribution and direct-airline retailing are real structural forces, but Amadeus is positioned as the *re-platformer* of the shift (NDC aggregation, Nevio offer/order, agentic-AI on its own data mesh) with deep switching costs; this is a fear-print on an entrenched rail, not a melting base — *for now*. It crosses to *material* if look-to-book economics break GDS unit pricing or a tech-native captures airline retailing at scale.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: WIDE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

# Forensic Dossier — Amadeus IT Group (AMS.MC)

*Five consecutive earnings calls reviewed: full-year 2024 results (Feb 28, 2025), Q1 2025 (May 8, 2025), first-half 2025 (Aug 1, 2025), Q3 2025 (Nov 7, 2025), and full-year 2025 results plus the new midterm outlook (Feb 27, 2026). Amadeus is the Madrid-listed travel-technology backbone — the "toll road" that connects airlines, hotels, travel agencies and airports. It is not a semiconductor company despite the ticker. Financials are from our screener scan, with the latest-quarter figures from the trailing-twelve-month block.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story is remarkably consistent across these five calls — which is itself a finding. Amadeus is a steady, double-digit-growing infrastructure business, and management talks like the custodian of one. The opening recap (full-year 2024) led with "double digit growth and expanding profitability," 13% revenue growth, and a fresh €1.3 billion buyback aimed at mopping up shares issued during the pandemic. By the close of this window (full-year 2025), the headline had shifted only slightly in tone — to "we have reached a tipping point" on Nevio, its next-generation airline-retailing platform — but the underlying message was the same: grow the toll road, invest heavily, return the rest.

Three threads run through every call. First, **Nevio / Navitaire Stratos** — the modernization of how airlines sell tickets (moving from old fare-filing to "offers and orders"). This thread *strengthened* materially over the year: from "four customers" (Air France-KLM joining BA, Saudia, Finnair) in early 2025 to the February 2026 announcement that nine Lufthansa Group airlines plan to adopt Nevio, plus TUI and Volotea on the low-cost Stratos product, and management's claim that "25% of Altéa passengers boarded are engaged in a Nevio program." Second, **NDC aggregation** (a new airline-content standard) — steady, almost ritual progress, from ~70 signed agreements early to "over 75" by year-end, with the honest admission that adoption as a *percentage* stays flat because every new airline enlarges the denominator. Third, **AI** — the emphasis here grew loudest, evolving from "we've used AI for 20 years" boilerplate into a genuine strategic frame by Q4 2025: Amadeus wants to be "the orchestrator in an AI-enabled travel ecosystem… the essential infrastructure powering" AI travel assistants.

What was quietly *dropped*: nothing was abandoned, but the pandemic-recovery framing ("post-COVID re-engagement," buyback to undo crisis dilution) faded as the recovery normalized, replaced by a more mature "high single-digit revenue / low double-digit EPS" midterm algorithm announced in February 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Double-digit growth and expanding profitability" (FY24) | Revenue 2024 €6.14B (+12.6% over 2023's €5.44B); 2025 €6.52B (+6.1% reported, but management cites +9% at constant currency) | **Matches on a constant-currency basis.** The gap between the reported +6.1% and management's "+9%" is foreign-exchange (a strong dollar/euro swing they flagged repeatedly), not narrative inflation. Honest. |
| "Free cash flow generation expanded to €1.3 billion" (FY24), then €1.3B again in 2025 "+7% excluding non-recurring" | Screener: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow €1.74B; full-year free-cash-flow margin a rich 32.1%; FCF grew +54% year-over-year on the scan and +33.8% on a three-year basis | **Confirmed and arguably understated by management.** This is a genuine cash machine. The 32% free-cash-flow margin is the single most important number in the file. |
| "Profit grew faster than revenue" (H1 25, repeated) | EPS €3.01 (2025) vs €2.79 (2024), +7.9%; net margin 20.5%; three-year EPS compound growth +27.6% | **Confirmed.** Operating leverage is real — EBIT growth (+10–15% constant currency) consistently outran revenue. |
| Margins "expanding" | Net margin 20.5% is healthy, but the scan flags **gross margin 27.8% and contracting**, and notes margin sits 0.57 standard deviations *below* its historical peak | **Mixed — a caution.** Headline profitability is strong and EBIT is expanding, but the gross line is under pressure from mix (more low-cost-carrier and local/domestic content carries lower unit economics, which management openly conceded: revenue-per-booking growth "will soften slightly" in 2026). The "expansion" is being engineered through cost discipline and the end of the cloud migration, not pricing. |
| Returns justify the "toll road moat" framing | ROE 17.6%, but **ROIC just 9.9%** | **The weak spot.** A return on invested capital under 10% is modest for a business sold as a wide-moat monopoly-like platform. The heavy R&D (over €1.4B in 2025, ~20% of revenue) and €2.68B of net debt are dragging invested-capital returns. The moat is real in switching-cost terms, but the *returns evidence* is good-not-great. |
| Buyback discipline | €1.3B buyback completed in Q4 2025, explicitly to redeem pandemic-era shares | **Confirmed and shareholder-friendly**, though note this was share-count repair, not aggressive value-accretive shrinkage. |

The overall read: the narrative is **honest and slightly conservative**, not promotional. Where management says "constant currency," they mean it, and the cash flows back them up. The one place the story is *richer than the numbers* is the moat/returns framing — a 9.9% return on capital does not scream "uncrossable moat."

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, with rising confidence specifically on Nevio.**

- **FY24 (Feb 2025):** Measured, delivery-focused. "We successfully deliver on our outlook and commitments." Offensive posture (investing for the future, cloud transformation).
- **Q1 2025 (May):** A notch more defensive on the macro — "despite the broad uncertainty in the environment" — and a tactical retreat to guiding *ex-foreign-exchange* because dollar/euro volatility was "beyond what we could foresee." Volumes "came in a bit below, but nevertheless quite good." This is the most hedged call in the set, and it coincided with the softest booking growth (+2.5%).
- **H1 2025 (Aug):** Continued macro caution (geopolitics, U.S. travel softness, a France controller strike, the Israel-Iran conflict) but a hopeful pivot: "hopefully we have seen the bottom of this deceleration."
- **Q3 2025 (Nov):** Tone clearly *lifted* — "a strong third quarter full of momentum, which drove revenue growth acceleration and margin expansion."
- **FY25 (Feb 2026):** The most confident call in the window. "We have reached a tipping point" on Nevio; a clean, specific three-part midterm algorithm; AI reframed as opportunity, not threat.

The arc is offensive → briefly defensive (mid-2025 macro wobble) → offensive again, ending on a high. Guidance got *more* specific over time (the February 2026 midterm targets are the most concrete commitment in the file).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest part of the dossier. Management set an ex-foreign-exchange 2025 outlook in May 2025 and, by February 2026, stated plainly: "we successfully delivered on our '25 outlook… achieving our 2025 guidance across all metrics." The screener corroborates a 6-of-7-quarter earnings-beat rate (86%). When they warned of weaker first-half free cash flow on working-capital and capital-expenditure timing (Q1 25), the second-half reacceleration they promised did materialize (full-year FCF landed at €1.3B). There is a mild *sandbagging* flavor — they repeatedly called their own three-year air-distribution compound-growth target "conservative" (Deutsche Bank pushed on exactly this in early 2025), and they tend to under-promise on currency by guiding constant-currency. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring analyst worries, and how management handled them:

- **Nevio deal pace.** The most persistent pressure point. Rothschild (Nov 2025): "we haven't seen a new customer for a while… are you comfortable with the current pace?" Management deflected to "engagement is high… nothing is done until it's really done." This was *answered* three months later by the Lufthansa/TUI/Volotea wins — so the worry was legitimate but resolved favorably. The risk: deal timing is genuinely lumpy and outside management's control ("it's a matter of priorities for the carriers").
- **Free-cash-flow seasonality.** JP Morgan pressed twice on first-half FCF being down year-over-year. Management's answer (working capital, tax timing, capex ramp) held up — full-year delivered.
- **Pricing durability.** Kepler Cheuvreux repeatedly asked whether the +5% revenue-per-booking growth is sustainable. Management was candid that the one-off boost from converting "full-content" to "relevant-content" agreements will fade and 2026 revenue-per-booking will "soften slightly." This is the honest admission of a *decelerating* pricing lever — worth weighting.
- **AI as threat vs. tool.** Bernstein (Feb 2026) pushed hard on whether AI coding tools should let R&D spend *plateau*. Management said no — capex stays low-double-digit (though declining as a share) — framing AI as "force multiplication," not cost-out. The subtext: the spending floor stays high.

No question turned into a later disaster within this window. The deflections were on timing, not substance.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Gross margin contracting** (27.8%, flagged "contracting") on adverse content mix (more low-cost-carrier / local bookings dilute unit economics) — the pricing tailwind is lapping.
🔴 **Return on invested capital below 10%** (9.9%) despite a premium "moat" narrative — heavy R&D and €2.68B net debt weigh on capital efficiency.
🔴 **Revenue-per-booking growth explicitly guided to soften** in 2026 (management's own words) — a known deceleration of a key lever.
🔴 **Volume is macro-hostage** — bookings and passengers-boarded swung with geopolitics (Mideast, U.S. softness, strikes) through 2025; management cannot control air traffic.

🟢 **Free-cash-flow margin of 32%** and trailing free cash flow of €1.74B — elite cash conversion.
🟢 **Guidance delivered in full** for 2025; 86% beat rate; a clear new midterm algorithm.
🟢 **Nevio reached genuine commercial scale** — Lufthansa Group (9 airlines), British Airways, Air France-KLM all engaged; 25% of Altéa passengers in a Nevio program; this is the durable growth engine working.
🟢 **AI positioned as ally** — "the essential infrastructure powering" AI travel assistants, with Google and Microsoft as named partners and the first travel "data mesh." Credible, not hand-wavy.
🟢 **Net leverage minimal** — 0.8–0.9x EBITDA; the €2.68B net debt is trivially serviced by €1.7B+ of annual free cash flow.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **A new CFO (Carol/Caroline Borg, started May 2025) brought a cleaner, more numbers-forward communication style** — she explicitly said she was "increasing transparency" on traffic assumptions and gave crisper guidance bridges. New voices that *add* disclosure are a green signal.
- **The terminology shifted from "GDS / distribution" toward "orchestrator of an AI-enabled travel ecosystem."** This is a deliberate repositioning ahead of the obvious bear question — whether AI agents disintermediate the middleman. Management is getting in front of it, framing Amadeus as the neutral data/infrastructure layer agents *need*, not the layer they replace. The Skylink acquisition (conversational-AI capability) reinforces this.
- **Capital allocation language is widening.** By Q3 2025 the CFO listed M&A as "a really key relevant part of our growth strategy" alongside buybacks and dividends, and promised a February budget update — a subtle signal that fresh capital-return or deal decisions are pending, not that a special situation is imminent.
- **The honest "disintermediation is real but we offset it" admission** (Q3 2025) on full-service carriers selling more direct — management neither denied the structural pressure nor panicked, which reads as credible.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Over these five calls the franchise got stronger on every axis that matters — Nevio crossed from pilot to scale, guidance was delivered in full, free cash flow compounded, and management got ahead of the AI question rather than ducking it. This is a high-quality, cash-generative infrastructure compounder run by a credible, slightly conservative team.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** this is a *quality-compounder-at-a-fair-price*, not a special situation. There is no dated catalyst, no activist, no asset sale, no forced selling. The entire return case rests on (a) the market continuing to re-rate a steady ~8% revenue / low-double-digit EPS grower toward its intrinsic value, and (b) the AI-agent disintermediation fear *not* proving terminal. The valuation is the edge (price-to-free-cash-flow ~10x, well below this asset's history and quality), but with no forcing function the convergence is slow and depends on macro travel demand staying healthy. Size it as a patient quality holding, not a catalyst trade.

**Economic moat: WIDE but the returns evidence is only NARROW-confirming — call it NARROW-to-WIDE, trend STABLE.** The moat type is genuine **switching-costs plus network/scale** — airlines, agencies and hotels are deeply integrated into Amadeus's core systems (25-year Ryanair relationship; "natively integrated… others cannot easily replicate"). That is real lock-in. *But* the hard returns evidence tempers the width: a 9.9% return on invested capital and a *contracting* gross margin are not the fingerprints of a widening, uncrossable moat — they are the fingerprints of a strong franchise spending heavily to defend and extend its position. The moat is durable, not expanding.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** The relevant structural force is AI-driven disintermediation (the "AI-displacement" tail — could AI agents route around the travel middleman?). The evidence says *manageable*: bookings and passengers-boarded are still *growing*, management is positioning as the AI infrastructure layer rather than the disrupted incumbent, and the switching costs are deep enough that a wholesale bypass is a multi-year, not imminent, risk. This is a fear-print / mispricing, not a structurally shrinking base — the cheapness reflects macro-travel uncertainty and a generalized "is AI coming for the middleman" worry, against a business whose volumes are still rising. It is *not* a value trap, but the AI question is the one that would change the rating if the evidence turned.

Amadeus is the plumbing of the travel industry: it runs the reservation systems airlines and hotels sell through (a global distribution system, or GDS, plus airline and hospitality IT). Across the four calls the core story stayed remarkably consistent — steady high-single-digit revenue growth, profit growing faster than revenue, and heavy reinvestment — but the *emphasis* shifted in three telling ways.

First, the growth engine broadened from "bookings recover after the pandemic" to "we are re-platforming the whole industry." Early in 2025 (February call) management led with volume: air distribution up 11% for 2024, bookings up, revenue-per-booking up ~5%. By the third-quarter 2025 call the lead had moved to *Nevio* — the next-generation, cloud-native airline retailing platform — and to agentic artificial intelligence (AI that can act, not just answer). The company went from describing AI as a 20-year-old internal tool to positioning itself as the entity "uniquely placed to infuse Agentic AI across the travel ecosystem."

Second, the tone on volumes turned quietly defensive. February 2025 boasted of 9-14% booking growth; by the first half of 2025 bookings were growing ~2.5-3.2% after stripping out calendar noise, and management spent real airtime explaining leap-year days, Easter/Ramadan timing, air-traffic "normalization," and one-off shocks (a Myanmar earthquake, U.S. government developments, a France controller strike, the Israel-Iran conflict). The underlying booking trend decelerated through the year — "April was better than May and May was better than June" (first-half 2025 call) — before management claimed to see "the bottom" in July.

Third, capital allocation moved from buyback-to-neutralize-dilution toward a genuine choice between buybacks and mergers-and-acquisitions. The €1.3B buyback launched in early 2025 was explicitly framed as cleaning up the 2020 convertible-bond dilution. By the November 2025 call the new chief financial officer was describing a "disciplined capital allocation policy" that keeps M&A as "a really key relevant part of our growth strategy" — foreshadowing the €1.2B IDEMIA Public Security biometrics acquisition announced April 2026.

|---|---|---|

Financials are from our screener scan, with the latest-quarter figures from the trailing-twelve-month block.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story is remarkably consistent across these five calls — which is itself a finding. Amadeus is a steady, double-digit-growing infrastructure business, and management talks like the custodian of one. The opening recap (full-year 2024) led with "double digit growth and expanding profitability," 13% revenue growth, and a fresh €1.3 billion buyback aimed at mopping up shares issued during the pandemic. 🔴 **Revenue-per-booking growth explicitly guided to soften** in 2026 (management's own words) — a known deceleration of a key lever.

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Over these five calls the franchise got stronger on every axis that matters — Nevio crossed from pilot to scale, guidance was delivered in full, free cash flow compounded, and management got ahead of the AI question rather than ducking it. This is a high-quality, cash-generative infrastructure compounder run by a credible, slightly conservative team.

There is no dated catalyst, no activist, no asset sale, no forced selling. The entire return case rests on (a) the market continuing to re-rate a steady ~8% revenue / low-double-digit EPS grower toward its intrinsic value, and (b) the AI-agent disintermediation fear *not* proving terminal. The valuation is the edge (price-to-free-cash-flow ~10x, well below this asset's history and quality), but with no forcing function the convergence is slow and depends on macro travel demand staying healthy. forcing_function: There is no hard, dated forcing event. The genuine re-rating driver would be evidence over several quarters that agentic AI is not disintermediating the distribution take-rate — an unfolding condition, not an event. For a deep-value name the classic forcing functions (activist, asset sale, dividend initiation, buyback authorization surprise) are either absent or already known. This is why the catalyst is best read as soft and non-binding.
valley_of_death: The near-term risk is not a cash-burn or maturity wall — the balance sheet is sound (~1x leverage, Altman-Z 3.0, 677M euros cash) and there is no debt cliff. It is not a yield vehicle whose holders would liquidate on a dividend change (the ~2.5% dividend is stable and was just paid), nor a spin-off stub or index-orphan facing calendar-driven flows, nor a leveraged name facing covenant pressure. The shareholder register is unlikely to turn over abruptly. This removes the single most attractive feature of a special situation — a captive, price-insensitive seller creating a dislocation — and is a core reason this is not an aggressive-entry setup.
moderator_conclusion: Amadeus is a genuinely high-quality, cash-generative travel-infrastructure franchise trading at a fair-to-modestly-cheap price — but it is not the special situation this book is built to reward, and the current regime makes that gap decisive. The market regime as of early July 2026 explicitly prizes hard-dated, resolution-independent special situations (forced-sellers, spin-offs, distressed) in thin-coverage lanes, and penalizes theses that hinge on a single shared macro or secular factor. The verdict is to pass for now: the value case is real but the discount is mostly earned, there is no catalyst to force convergence, and the regime rewards putting capital where a dated event does the work. # Forensic Dossier — Amadeus IT Group (AMS.MC)

*Five consecutive earnings calls reviewed: full-year 2024 results (Feb 28, 2025), Q1 2025 (May 8, 2025), first-half 2025 (Aug 1, 2025), Q3 2025 (Nov 7, 2025), and full-year 2025 results plus the new midterm outlook (Feb 27, 2026). Amadeus is the Madrid-listed travel-technology backbone — the "toll road" that connects airlines, hotels, travel agencies and airports. It is not a semiconductor company despite the ticker. Financials are from our screener scan, with the latest-quarter figures from the trailing-twelve-month block.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story is remarkably consistent across these five calls — which is itself a finding. Amadeus is a steady, double-digit-growing infrastructure business, and management talks like the custodian of one. The opening recap (full-year 2024) led with "double digit growth and expanding profitability," 13% revenue growth, and a fresh €1.3 billion buyback aimed at mopping up shares issued during the pandemic. By the close of this window (full-year 2025), the headline had shifted only slightly in tone — to "we have reached a tipping point" on Nevio, its next-generation airline-retailing platform — but the underlying message was the same: grow the toll road, invest heavily, return the rest.

Three threads run through every call. First, **Nevio / Navitaire Stratos** — the modernization of how airlines sell tickets (moving from old fare-filing to "offers and orders"). This thread *strengthened* materially over the year: from "four customers" (Air France-KLM joining BA, Saudia, Finnair) in early 2025 to the February 2026 announcement that nine Lufthansa Group airlines plan to adopt Nevio, plus TUI and Volotea on the low-cost Stratos product, and management's claim that "25% of Altéa passengers boarded are engaged in a Nevio program." Second, **NDC aggregation** (a new airline-content standard) — steady, almost ritual progress, from ~70 signed agreements early to "over 75" by year-end, with the honest admission that adoption as a *percentage* stays flat because every new airline enlarges the denominator. Third, **AI** — the emphasis here grew loudest, evolving from "we've used AI for 20 years" boilerplate into a genuine strategic frame by Q4 2025: Amadeus wants to be "the orchestrator in an AI-enabled travel ecosystem… the essential infrastructure powering" AI travel assistants.

What was quietly *dropped*: nothing was abandoned, but the pandemic-recovery framing ("post-COVID re-engagement," buyback to undo crisis dilution) faded as the recovery normalized, replaced by a more mature "high single-digit revenue / low double-digit EPS" midterm algorithm announced in February 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Double-digit growth and expanding profitability" (FY24) | Revenue 2024 €6.14B (+12.6% over 2023's €5.44B); 2025 €6.52B (+6.1% reported, but management cites +9% at constant currency) | **Matches on a constant-currency basis.** The gap between the reported +6.1% and management's "+9%" is foreign-exchange (a strong dollar/euro swing they flagged repeatedly), not narrative inflation. Honest. |
| "Free cash flow generation expanded to €1.3 billion" (FY24), then €1.3B again in 2025 "+7% excluding non-recurring" | Screener: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow €1.74B; full-year free-cash-flow margin a rich 32.1%; FCF grew +54% year-over-year on the scan and +33.8% on a three-year basis | **Confirmed and arguably understated by management.** This is a genuine cash machine. The 32% free-cash-flow margin is the single most important number in the file. |
| "Profit grew faster than revenue" (H1 25, repeated) | EPS €3.01 (2025) vs €2.79 (2024), +7.9%; net margin 20.5%; three-year EPS compound growth +27.6% | **Confirmed.** Operating leverage is real — EBIT growth (+10–15% constant currency) consistently outran revenue. |
| Margins "expanding" | Net margin 20.5% is healthy, but the scan flags **gross margin 27.8% and contracting**, and notes margin sits 0.57 standard deviations *below* its historical peak | **Mixed — a caution.** Headline profitability is strong and EBIT is expanding, but the gross line is under pressure from mix (more low-cost-carrier and local/domestic content carries lower unit economics, which management openly conceded: revenue-per-booking growth "will soften slightly" in 2026). The "expansion" is being engineered through cost discipline and the end of the cloud migration, not pricing. |
| Returns justify the "toll road moat" framing | ROE 17.6%, but **ROIC just 9.9%** | **The weak spot.** A return on invested capital under 10% is modest for a business sold as a wide-moat monopoly-like platform. The heavy R&D (over €1.4B in 2025, ~20% of revenue) and €2.68B of net debt are dragging invested-capital returns. The moat is real in switching-cost terms, but the *returns evidence* is good-not-great. |
| Buyback discipline | €1.3B buyback completed in Q4 2025, explicitly to redeem pandemic-era shares | **Confirmed and shareholder-friendly**, though note this was share-count repair, not aggressive value-accretive shrinkage. |

The overall read: the narrative is **honest and slightly conservative**, not promotional. Where management says "constant currency," they mean it, and the cash flows back them up. The one place the story is *richer than the numbers* is the moat/returns framing — a 9.9% return on capital does not scream "uncrossable moat."

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, with rising confidence specifically on Nevio.**

- **FY24 (Feb 2025):** Measured, delivery-focused. "We successfully deliver on our outlook and commitments." Offensive posture (investing for the future, cloud transformation).
- **Q1 2025 (May):** A notch more defensive on the macro — "despite the broad uncertainty in the environment" — and a tactical retreat to guiding *ex-foreign-exchange* because dollar/euro volatility was "beyond what we could foresee." Volumes "came in a bit below, but nevertheless quite good." This is the most hedged call in the set, and it coincided with the softest booking growth (+2.5%).
- **H1 2025 (Aug):** Continued macro caution (geopolitics, U.S. travel softness, a France controller strike, the Israel-Iran conflict) but a hopeful pivot: "hopefully we have seen the bottom of this deceleration."
- **Q3 2025 (Nov):** Tone clearly *lifted* — "a strong third quarter full of momentum, which drove revenue growth acceleration and margin expansion."
- **FY25 (Feb 2026):** The most confident call in the window. "We have reached a tipping point" on Nevio; a clean, specific three-part midterm algorithm; AI reframed as opportunity, not threat.

The arc is offensive → briefly defensive (mid-2025 macro wobble) → offensive again, ending on a high. Guidance got *more* specific over time (the February 2026 midterm targets are the most concrete commitment in the file).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** This is the strongest part of the dossier. Management set an ex-foreign-exchange 2025 outlook in May 2025 and, by February 2026, stated plainly: "we successfully delivered on our '25 outlook… achieving our 2025 guidance across all metrics." The screener corroborates a 6-of-7-quarter earnings-beat rate (86%). When they warned of weaker first-half free cash flow on working-capital and capital-expenditure timing (Q1 25), the second-half reacceleration they promised did materialize (full-year FCF landed at €1.3B). There is a mild *sandbagging* flavor — they repeatedly called their own three-year air-distribution compound-growth target "conservative" (Deutsche Bank pushed on exactly this in early 2025), and they tend to under-promise on currency by guiding constant-currency. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring analyst worries, and how management handled them:

- **Nevio deal pace.** The most persistent pressure point. Rothschild (Nov 2025): "we haven't seen a new customer for a while… are you comfortable with the current pace?" Management deflected to "engagement is high… nothing is done until it's really done." This was *answered* three months later by the Lufthansa/TUI/Volotea wins — so the worry was legitimate but resolved favorably. The risk: deal timing is genuinely lumpy and outside management's control ("it's a matter of priorities for the carriers").
- **Free-cash-flow seasonality.** JP Morgan pressed twice on first-half FCF being down year-over-year. Management's answer (working capital, tax timing, capex ramp) held up — full-year delivered.
- **Pricing durability.** Kepler Cheuvreux repeatedly asked whether the +5% revenue-per-booking growth is sustainable. Management was candid that the one-off boost from converting "full-content" to "relevant-content" agreements will fade and 2026 revenue-per-booking will "soften slightly." This is the honest admission of a *decelerating* pricing lever — worth weighting.
- **AI as threat vs. tool.** Bernstein (Feb 2026) pushed hard on whether AI coding tools should let R&D spend *plateau*. Management said no — capex stays low-double-digit (though declining as a share) — framing AI as "force multiplication," not cost-out. The subtext: the spending floor stays high.

No question turned into a later disaster within this window. The deflections were on timing, not substance.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Gross margin contracting** (27.8%, flagged "contracting") on adverse content mix (more low-cost-carrier / local bookings dilute unit economics) — the pricing tailwind is lapping.
🔴 **Return on invested capital below 10%** (9.9%) despite a premium "moat" narrative — heavy R&D and €2.68B net debt weigh on capital efficiency.
🔴 **Revenue-per-booking growth explicitly guided to soften** in 2026 (management's own words) — a known deceleration of a key lever.
🔴 **Volume is macro-hostage** — bookings and passengers-boarded swung with geopolitics (Mideast, U.S. softness, strikes) through 2025; management cannot control air traffic.

🟢 **Free-cash-flow margin of 32%** and trailing free cash flow of €1.74B — elite cash conversion.
🟢 **Guidance delivered in full** for 2025; 86% beat rate; a clear new midterm algorithm.
🟢 **Nevio reached genuine commercial scale** — Lufthansa Group (9 airlines), British Airways, Air France-KLM all engaged; 25% of Altéa passengers in a Nevio program; this is the durable growth engine working.
🟢 **AI positioned as ally** — "the essential infrastructure powering" AI travel assistants, with Google and Microsoft as named partners and the first travel "data mesh." Credible, not hand-wavy.
🟢 **Net leverage minimal** — 0.8–0.9x EBITDA; the €2.68B net debt is trivially serviced by €1.7B+ of annual free cash flow.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **A new CFO (Carol/Caroline Borg, started May 2025) brought a cleaner, more numbers-forward communication style** — she explicitly said she was "increasing transparency" on traffic assumptions and gave crisper guidance bridges. New voices that *add* disclosure are a green signal.
- **The terminology shifted from "GDS / distribution" toward "orchestrator of an AI-enabled travel ecosystem."** This is a deliberate repositioning ahead of the obvious bear question — whether AI agents disintermediate the middleman. Management is getting in front of it, framing Amadeus as the neutral data/infrastructure layer agents *need*, not the layer they replace. The Skylink acquisition (conversational-AI capability) reinforces this.
- **Capital allocation language is widening.** By Q3 2025 the CFO listed M&A as "a really key relevant part of our growth strategy" alongside buybacks and dividends, and promised a February budget update — a subtle signal that fresh capital-return or deal decisions are pending, not that a special situation is imminent.
- **The honest "disintermediation is real but we offset it" admission** (Q3 2025) on full-service carriers selling more direct — management neither denied the structural pressure nor panicked, which reads as credible.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Over these five calls the franchise got stronger on every axis that matters — Nevio crossed from pilot to scale, guidance was delivered in full, free cash flow compounded, and management got ahead of the AI question rather than ducking it. This is a high-quality, cash-generative infrastructure compounder run by a credible, slightly conservative team.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** this is a *quality-compounder-at-a-fair-price*, not a special situation. There is no dated catalyst, no activist, no asset sale, no forced selling. The entire return case rests on (a) the market continuing to re-rate a steady ~8% revenue / low-double-digit EPS grower toward its intrinsic value, and (b) the AI-agent disintermediation fear *not* proving terminal. The valuation is the edge (price-to-free-cash-flow ~10x, well below this asset's history and quality), but with no forcing function the convergence is slow and depends on macro travel demand staying healthy. Size it as a patient quality holding, not a catalyst trade.

**Economic moat: WIDE but the returns evidence is only NARROW-confirming — call it NARROW-to-WIDE, trend STABLE.** The moat type is genuine **switching-costs plus network/scale** — airlines, agencies and hotels are deeply integrated into Amadeus's core systems (25-year Ryanair relationship; "natively integrated… others cannot easily replicate"). That is real lock-in. *But* the hard returns evidence tempers the width: a 9.9% return on invested capital and a *contracting* gross margin are not the fingerprints of a widening, uncrossable moat — they are the fingerprints of a strong franchise spending heavily to defend and extend its position. The moat is durable, not expanding.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, not terminal.** The relevant structural force is AI-driven disintermediation (the "AI-displacement" tail — could AI agents route around the travel middleman?). The evidence says *manageable*: bookings and passengers-boarded are still *growing*, management is positioning as the AI infrastructure layer rather than the disrupted incumbent, and the switching costs are deep enough that a wholesale bypass is a multi-year, not imminent, risk. This is a fear-print / mispricing, not a structurally shrinking base — the cheapness reflects macro-travel uncertainty and a generalized "is AI coming for the middleman" worry, against a business whose volumes are still rising. It is *not* a value trap, but the AI question is the one that would change the rating if the evidence turned.
